name: Gajendra
role: Elephant king rescued by Vishnu in the Bhagavata Purana
summary: Gajendra is the elephant king in the Bhagavata Purana whose long struggle with a crocodile ends when he calls on Vishnu. The tale, called Gajendra Moksha, is one of the best-loved Puranic stories.
about: In the Bhagavata Purana (Canto 8), Gajendra is the leader of a herd of elephants living on Mount Trikuta. When he enters a lotus lake to bathe, a crocodile seizes his leg and the two struggle for a thousand years. The text says that in his earlier life he was Indradyumna, a Pandya king and devotee of Vishnu, whom the sage Agastya cursed to be born as an elephant. The crocodile was once a gandharva named Huhu, cursed by the sage Devala. As his strength fails, Gajendra offers a lotus and calls on Vishnu, who arrives on Garuda and frees him. Many Vaishnava readers see the tale as a picture of a soul that finds freedom by sincere surrender. The story is told by the sage Shuka to King Parikshit.
kidSummary: Gajendra is a big, strong elephant who gets caught by a crocodile in a lake. His herd cannot help him, and he gets very tired. Then he lifts a lotus flower and asks Vishnu for help, and Vishnu comes quickly to rescue him.

story.title: A lake on Mount Trikuta
story.text: Gajendra is the king of a herd of elephants. One hot day they all go to a beautiful lotus lake on Mount Trikuta to drink and splash.

story.title: Caught!
story.text: While Gajendra is bathing, a crocodile grabs his leg and will not let go. The two pull and pull, and the tale says it lasts for a thousand years.

story.title: Nobody can help
story.text: His family and friends try to pull him out but cannot. Gajendra grows tired and weak while the crocodile only grows stronger.

story.title: A lotus and a prayer
story.text: Gajendra stops trusting his own strength. He lifts a lotus flower in his trunk and calls to Vishnu with a heartfelt prayer.

story.title: Vishnu arrives
story.text: Vishnu comes swiftly on Garuda, lifts Gajendra and the crocodile out of the water, and with his discus severs the crocodile's mouth from its body. Both are freed from their old curses.

teaches: When you cannot do it alone, ask for help
The story teaches that sincere prayer is heard

family.relation: Cursed him in a past life
family.name: Agastya

texts: Gajendra Mokshamu in Pothana's Telugu Bhagavatam
places: Gajendra Varadha Temple, Kapisthalam, Tamil Nadu
festivals: Gajendra Moksha Leela at Kapisthalam (Tamil month of Aadi)

facts.text: Seeing Gajendra in pain, Vishnu climbs down from Garuda and pulls the elephant and the crocodile out of the lake together; the verse says he cut the crocodile's mouth away from its body with his discus (Bhagavata 8.3.33).

The Bhagavata says Mount Trikuta is ringed by the Ocean of Milk, is ten thousand yojanas high, and has peaks of iron, silver and gold; Gajendra's lake lies in Ritumat, Varuna's garden there, full of golden lotuses, swans and humming bees.

The Gajendra Moksha niche on the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh was carved about 1,500 years ago, around 500 CE, on what is called one of the oldest surviving Hindu stone temples; it shows the elephant holding a lotus in a pond while Vishnu flies in on Garuda.

Sonepur, where the Gandak meets the Ganga, is linked to the legend, which places the fight's end beside the Harihar Nath temple; elephants are still lined up at its fair though they cannot legally be sold, and the count fell from 354 in 2004 to 3 in 2017.

The Bhagavata says that as King Indradyumna, a Pandya ascetic of the Malaya Hills, Gajendra was cursed by Agastya into an elephant for not welcoming him; yet in his hour of need he recalled a prayer from that life and began by bowing to the Lord (8.3.1).

A summary of Bhagavata chapter 8.4 tells that the crocodile was Huhu, a gandharva who playfully tugged the sage Devala's leg while bathing; the verses themselves say Devala cursed him to become a crocodile.

Gajendra and the crocodile were not evenly matched: the Bhagavata says that in the water, foreign to the elephant, his body, mind and senses weakened, while the water-born crocodile kept finding food and grew stronger (8.2.30).
The Bhagavata says the gods did not come because Gajendra's prayer named no particular god; he was calling on the Supreme above all, so the Lord himself answered (8.3.30).

Versions differ: the Bhagavata names Agastya as the cursing sage, while the Kapisthalam temple tradition names Durvasa and calls the crocodile Kuhu; there Gajendra cries out Adimulam, the primal source, as the crocodile seizes his leg.
The Bhagavata says that reciting this story on waking, or praying as Gajendra did, helps keep bad dreams away and protects from the harm of Kali yuga.

A Telugu tradition says Pothana wrote only the first line of his Gajendra verse, about Vaikuntha, then went to farm; he returned to find it finished, and his daughter said he had come by that afternoon and written it himself, so he concluded Rama had done it.
Before the crocodile, the text shows Gajendra as a strong herd leader: tigers and lions run from his scent, while foxes, deer and monkeys feel safe near him.

The Bhagavata places the rescue in the age of the fourth Manu, Tamasa, and says the avatar Hari, son of Harimedha and Harini, earned his name by saving the elephant-king from the crocodile (8.1.28-30).

Scholars note that the Kapisthalam temple, one of the 108 Divya Desams of Vishnu, is unusual because Vishnu is said to have come down here to rescue an animal; at other Vishnu temples he saves sages, celestial beings or demons.
Local tradition says Hanuman worshipped at Kapisthalam, and the village name is read as the place of the monkey, since kabi means monkey in Tamil.

Around 1871 the Deogarh temple with the Gajendra panel was found in dense jungle, and an 1875 survey report spread its fame; local memory said the ten avatars were carved there, and many of its panels were lost in the early twentieth century.

In the Bhagavata, once the crocodile seized him, the other elephants and his wives could not get a grip on it from behind, and Gajendra decided that no relative could save him, which is when he turned to the Lord (8.2.28-32).
The tale is carved on a wall of the BAPS Hindu Mandir in Abu Dhabi, and the Brooklyn Museum holds an artwork called Vishnu Saving the Elephant that shows it.
Many readers take the story as a picture: Gajendra stands for a person, the crocodile for wrongdoing, and the muddy lake for samsara, the cycle of rebirth.
After the rescue the Bhagavata says Gajendra received a form like Vishnu's, with four arms, and went to Vishnu's abode, while Huhu returned to his gandharva form (8.4).
At Kapisthalam the main Vishnu image is shown reclining in the sanctum, and the best-known of its yearly festivals is the Gajendra Moksha Leela in the Tamil month of Aadi (July to August).

quiz.q: Which sage cursed King Indradyumna to become an elephant in the Bhagavata?
quiz.why: The Bhagavata names Agastya; the Kapisthalam temple tradition names Durvasa.

quiz.q: What does Gajendra hold up when he calls to Vishnu?
quiz.why: He offers a lotus with his trunk.

quiz.q: Who carries Vishnu to the rescue in the story?
How long does the struggle last in the Bhagavata?
quiz.why: The text says a thousand years.

quiz.q: What was the crocodile in his earlier life?
quiz.why: Huhu, a gandharva, was cursed to become a crocodile.
